state.misconception_label: Does not understand that 2n represents an even number

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: Which of these shows part of the proof that the sum of two odd numbers is even? I got \( \begin{array}{l}2 n+(2 m+1) \\ =2(n+m)+1\end{array} \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think of it this way: if you have two pencils (2n) and then add one more pencil (2m+1), you would have a total of two pairs of pencils (2(n+m)) and one extra pencil. This demonstrates that the sum of two odd numbers is even. Can you see how this concrete example matches the algebraic expression you originally wrote out?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get what you're saying about the pencils. So, when I add 2n and 2m+1, it’s like I’m trying to make pairs, but I end up with one extra pencil. But I still don’t really understand why 2n is always even. Can you explain that part again?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you were pairing up pairs of socks (2n) and then adding one more sock (2m+1). You would end up with two complete pairs of socks (2(n+m)) and one leftover sock. This helps illustrate why the sum of two odd numbers is always even. Can you see how this relates to the algebraic expression you're working with?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher repeatedly ignores the student's explicit request in Turn 2 to explain why 2n is even, instead offering the same flawed concrete analogy that confuses the representation of odd numbers (using 2m+1 incorrectly) and fails to address the core misconception.
